task.name: Per-story budget should adapt to the story's complexity band instead of a fixed ceiling
task.story_text:
## Observed / motivation

The per-story budget is a fixed number (`budget_usd` in forge.yaml, $50 here). It
is partitioned by fixed percentages before any work begins — dev 60%, preflight
and synthesis a floor-bounded 2% each, and the remainder split evenly across the
seated reviewers. Nothing rebalances that partition afterwards, against actual
spend or against the sprint-level ceiling passed to `--budget`.

Story cost is not distributed in a way a single number can govern. Across the 327
scored story audits in this repository:

| complexity score | n | median | p90 | max |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2 | 24 | $0.46 | $1.08 | $1.35 |
| 3 | 45 | $1.07 | $3.09 | $7.55 |
| 4 | 48 | $1.43 | $4.65 | $8.14 |
| 5 | 54 | $3.21 | $8.57 | $18.49 |
| 6 | 58 | $3.83 | $14.16 | $28.83 |
| 7 | 29 | $7.60 | $20.37 | $28.09 |
| 8 | 53 | $7.68 | $22.26 | $41.80 |
| 9 | 15 | $7.53 | $19.74 | $40.64 |

Median cost rises roughly sixteenfold from score 2 to score 8. A flat $50 is
about a hundred times the median score-2 story and about 1.2 times the most
expensive score-8 story observed. It is therefore unable to detect a runaway on a
small story — which would have to exceed its expected cost by two orders of
magnitude before the cap noticed — while being close to binding on large stories
doing legitimate work.

Both halves of that have now been observed. Story #1415 (complexity score 9, a
60-file refactor) had four of five and then two of three reviewers excluded
mid-review for exceeding their derived share, escalating twice on an unreachable
quorum while the sprint it belonged to had spent $46 of a $120 ceiling. Searching
all 703 story audits, exactly one contains a budget-excluded reviewer attempt and
it is from that story; the cap has never bound before because nothing had been
expensive enough to reach it.

Raising the fixed number to accommodate the outlier makes it correspondingly less
able to catch a runaway on everything else.

The signal needed to do better is already computed and already trusted. The
preflight complexity score drives model tier and reviewer count today; budget is
the one axis that does not consult it. A routing-time cost governor also already
exists — `per_story_routing_cost_target` downgrades tiers to fit an estimated
total and records each adjustment in the routing rationale — but it is unset, and
it governs planning rather than runtime spend.

## Why

A runaway is a deviation from what a story of its kind normally costs, not an
absolute dollar amount. A score-2 story at $8 is anomalous; a score-9 story at
$40 is ordinary. A fixed ceiling classifies both incorrectly, and the failure it
produces when it does bind is silent participant exclusion rather than a report
that the story needed more than its configuration allowed.

## Acceptance criteria

- The per-story allocation is derived from the story's complexity score and the
  observed cost distribution for that score band in the audit substrate, rather
  than from a single configured constant.
- A score band with insufficient history falls back to the configured value, and
  the record states which basis was used.
- Exceeding the allocation is reported as an explicit condition naming the story,
  its expected range and its observed cost — distinguishable from a story that
  completed within budget and from one that failed for unrelated reasons.
- Reaching the allocation does not silently reduce the work performed; where a
  phase cannot be funded, the run says so rather than proceeding with fewer
  participants than it planned.
- Per-story spend is reported against both its own allocation and the remaining
  sprint ceiling, so an allocation shortfall occurring while sprint headroom
  remains is visible as such.
- The derivation is mechanical — computed from recorded costs and the existing
  score, with no model involvement.
- Tests cover a story within its band, a story exceeding it, a band with no
  history, and a story whose allocation is exhausted while sprint budget remains.

## Example

A story scored 2 whose cost passes $4 is flagged as anomalous, because the
observed median for that band is $0.46 and its p90 is $1.08. A story scored 9
reaching $40 is not flagged, because the observed maximum for that band is
$40.64. Today a single $50 ceiling treats the first as unremarkable and comes
close to constraining the second.

Supersedes #343, which proposed the reporting half of this (cost proportions,
anomaly detection, phase timing) as a separate mechanism. Related: #2154
(panel-size routing), #1108 (score-driven reasoning effort).

handoff.summary: Added a deterministic per-story budget allocator (src/theforge/coordinator/story_budget.py) that derives a story's dollar allocation from the observed cost distribution for its preflight complexity score, read from the audit substrate via a new derive_cost_samples_by_score reader that filters tainted runs through the existing centralized gate. The allocation is band max x 1.25 headroom with a $1 floor; a band below an 8-run sample floor falls back to the configured per-story budget (models_budget_usd, or the sum of configured role budgets on the legacy path) and records the basis and reason. _apply_preflight_config installs the allocation right after the complexity score is known and proportionally rescales the resolved runtime profile budgets (dev/preflight/plan/reviewers/synthesis) to it, keeping explicit forge.yaml overrides locked; the record is stored on CoordinatorState.story_allocation and mirrored into complexity_routing_audit so resume persistence carries it. Reviewer budget exclusion is replaced by telemetry: an over-share reviewer keeps its verdict, counts toward quorum, and the overrun is recorded in state.reviewer_budget_overruns with a budget_overrun attempt outcome. A phase-entry funding check in _run_review_pool escalates with error_type allocation_exhausted, naming the story, its allocation, expected range, observed cost and the planned participants, instead of seating a smaller panel. Reporting adds cost.story_allocation / allocation_exhausted / reviewer_budget_overruns to the per-run audit (schema 19 -> 20 with a paired reader migration and regenerated snapshot fixture), a story_allocation block on sprint story entries and sprint-summary rows joining the allocation with sprint budget/spend/remaining headroom, and a status-row annotation rendered only for an exceeded or exhausted allocation.

story_deviations: The allocation-exhausted message does not itself render remaining sprint headroom. CoordinatorState has no sprint-ceiling field (state.py notes budget governance lives at the sprint level), so the coordinator emits allocation/observed/expected and the sprint layer joins it against resolved.budget_usd on the story row — the plan reviewer's suggested option B. The message says explicitly that sprint headroom is reported alongside the story in the sprint summary.

Budget rescaling operates on the resolved runtime profiles rather than derive_roles(), which is only on the simple-mode config-load path and is not the runtime budget authority for adaptive runs. Both plan reviewers flagged this; the helper (scale_role_budgets) governs both paths.

The phase-entry funding check is wired into the review phase only. That is where the 'fewer participants than planned' failure mode exists (and where #1415 was observed); dev is a single participant, so an under-funded dev phase surfaces through existing budget behavior rather than as a panel reduction.
deferred_items: 17 tests fail in this sandbox (test_cut_rc_isolation.py, test_sprint_lock.py, test_sprint_reexec_collision.py) with 'Operation not permitted' from mktemp and multiprocessing semaphores. They fail identically on the unmodified tree and are environmental, not caused by this change.

handoff.summary: Iteration 2 addresses both carried P2 findings, which shared one root cause: the resume-carry of story_allocation was inert because --resume re-enters PREFLIGHT and _apply_story_allocation re-derived unconditionally, overwriting the restored value before any phase read it; routing recovery hit the same overwrite since it re-enters the same applier. Added _carried_story_allocation(state) in preflight.py, which returns an allocation already on state only when it was derived for the current complexity score, and made _apply_story_allocation reuse it instead of re-deriving. Re-derivation still happens when the band actually differs, so a resumed attempt that scores differently is never judged against another band's distribution. Per-role shares are recomputed on every entry because config is resolved fresh and a carried record's share map may not match the current roles. Fixed an adjacent bug the change exposed: _configured_story_budget was read unconditionally, but on a re-entry the profile sum is the PREVIOUS allocation rather than the operator's configured per-story budget, so a fallback derived on a second pass would have been silently wrong — it is now read only on the deriving path. A carried record is stamped carried: true so the audit distinguishes an inherited allocation from a derived one (convention 6). Three new seam tests cover the restored allocation surviving the resumed preflight (seeded so re-derivation would yield a visibly different number), a different band on resume being re-derived rather than inherited, and re-entry within one run neither redrawing the allocation nor corrupting the recorded fallback. No changes to the implementation's approach, the allocator, the review-pool funding check, or the reporting surfaces.

findings.description: When a resumed story has no cached preflight state but does have a persisted routing record, routing recovery re-derives the story allocation and can overwrite the allocation restored from the prior attempt's resume record.

apply_resume_record_to_state copies the persisted story_allocation onto state.story_allocation during run_setup, but on a normal --resume (without --from bypassing PREFLIGHT) the engine always re-invokes _run_preflight_phase, which calls _apply_preflight_config → _apply_story_allocation and unconditionally overwrites state.story_allocation with a freshly derived value before any phase consults it — the restored allocation from the resume record is never actually read by anything downstream.

plan_review.findings:
- [P1-impl] [anthropic-opus-cli] Step 1 lists src/theforge/coordinator/audit_substrate.py under Action: create, but that module already exists (2448 lines) and owns all sqlite3 access, schema bootstrap, and the migration chain (CURRENT_RECORD_SCHEMA_VERSION = 19). A literal create would destroy it. The step's Details text makes the actual intent clear (a new low-dependency helper that *uses* require_substrate/create_or_open), so this is a mislabel rather than a wrong design.
  Suggestion: Treat audit_substrate.py as modify (or leave untouched entirely) and confine new code to the new story_budget.py; add the band-distribution query as an additional query helper alongside the existing derive_assignment_history/latest_record_for readers rather than rewriting the module.
- [P1-impl] [anthropic-opus-cli] Step 3 wants the coordinator-side allocation-exhausted escalation message to name the 'remaining sprint headroom', but CoordinatorState has no sprint-ceiling field — state.py:873 explicitly notes that budget governance lives at the sprint level (forge.yaml budget_usd), and the ceiling only reaches evaluate_budget() at sprint/runner.py:5186. The coordinator cannot render headroom without new plumbing.
  Suggestion: Either pass the sprint ceiling/spend-so-far into the run (a new CoordinatorState field set at run construction, mirroring how sprint_name is already threaded), or have the coordinator emit allocation/observed-cost only and let sprint/runner.py join it against resolved.budget_usd when writing the per-story entry — the latter keeps the AC satisfied entirely within Step 4.
- [P2] [anthropic-opus-cli] Step 2 says to 'reuse the existing derive_roles budget partitioning behavior' inside _apply_preflight_config, but derive_roles() is only invoked on the simple-mode config-load path (config/load.py:1080); when config.assignment.enabled and config.agents are set, profiles come from assign_models and never pass through derive_roles' 60%/2%/2%/split partition.
  Suggestion: Make the rescale operate on the resolved profiles' budget_usd (proportional scaling of dev/preflight/synthesis/reviewer shares to the derived allocation) so both the simple-mode and assignment paths are governed, rather than assuming derive_roles is on the preflight code path.
- [P2] [google-gemini-3.5-flash-api] The plan does not specify the exact fallback logic when models_budget_usd is not set (e.g., when using the legacy profiles block). The fallback per-story budget should be robustly resolved from either config.models_budget_usd or the sum of the configured profiles' budgets. Step 1 mentions using the existing configured per-story budget_usd as fallback. Suggestion: Explicitly handle both the models_budget_usd path and the legacy profiles budget sum path when resolving the fallback configured value.
- [P1-impl] [openai-gpt-5.4-cli] Step 2 stores the allocation record on CoordinatorState and in complexity_routing_audit, but the plan does not explicitly call out the existing resume/phase-recovery persistence path in src/theforge/coordinator/resume_persistence.py. If the allocation basis must survive resume the same way complexity_routing_audit already does, that module will need to keep serializing/restoring the added state.
  Suggestion: During implementation, either keep the allocation data solely inside complexity_routing_audit/routing-derived audit blocks that resume_persistence already carries, or explicitly extend resume persistence for any new top-level CoordinatorState allocation field.
- [P1-impl] [openai-gpt-5.4-cli] Step 2 says to reuse derive_roles budget partitioning, but the active runtime routing path after preflight is assignment.assign_models() in src/theforge/coordinator/preflight.py and src/theforge/assignment.py, not derive_roles(). The plan is still workable, but the implementation must avoid assuming derive_roles() is the runtime budget authority for adaptive runs.
  Suggestion: Implement the shared budget split as a helper that can be applied to the post-assignment runtime profiles in _apply_preflight_config, while preserving the existing explicit-override and budget_audit behavior.

finding_registry.description: When a resumed story has no cached preflight state but does have a persisted routing record, routing recovery re-derives the story allocation and can overwrite the allocation restored from the prior attempt's resume record.

apply_resume_record_to_state copies the persisted story_allocation onto state.story_allocation during run_setup, but on a normal --resume (without --from bypassing PREFLIGHT) the engine always re-invokes _run_preflight_phase, which calls _apply_preflight_config → _apply_story_allocation and unconditionally overwrites state.story_allocation with a freshly derived value before any phase consults it — the restored allocation from the resume record is never actually read by anything downstream.

soft: Coordinator is pure Python — no LLM calls for routing or process decisions
Schema validation is the integrity boundary — do not relax cross-validation rules
Keep modules single-purpose; extract instead of growing monolith files
Keep pure-data types in low-dependency modules with stdlib-only imports
Separate prompt construction, output parsing, and coordinator control flow

When adding or modifying data that flows between coordinator phases, instrument the change so the actual values are visible in the audit trail — diagnosing sprint failures requires tracing real data, not reconstructing it
Do not create files outside src/, tests/, or docs/. If you need a scratch file for exploration, delete it before committing.

Changes that affect coordinator phase boundaries, state handoff between phases, or adaptive routing/config propagation must include seam-level integration tests covering the touched boundary. Unit tests alone are insufficient when correctness depends on cross-phase state flow.
